hints: Focus on what excess hot concentrated sulfuric acid does to alcohols, and count atoms to see how many waters must be lost.
Work out the first dehydration for compound 1, the ring OH can only form a C=C in the ring in one symmetrical way.
Compare the 1,2 positions in compound 2 with the 1,3 and 1,4 positions, and ask whether different C=C positions give the same diene or different dienes.
walkthrough:
**Recognise double dehydration**

Each starting diol has formula $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2$. Heating with excess concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ eliminates water from each $\text{-OH}$ group.

$$\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_7\text{H}_{10} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Understand the two eliminations**

The secondary ring $\text{-OH}$ loses $\text{-OH}$ plus a H from an adjacent ring carbon to give a cyclohexene. The primary $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ loses $\text{-OH}$ plus a H from the ring carbon it is attached to, to give an exocyclic $\text{C=CH}_2$ group. The final product is therefore a methylenecyclohexene diene.

**Check compound 1 for symmetry**

In 1, the $\text{OH}$ is at C1 and $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is at C4, opposite each other. Loss of H from C2 or C6 to form the ring $\text{C=C}$ gives the same intermediate by symmetry, and the second elimination can only give 4-methylenecyclohex-1-ene. So only one $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{10}$ product.

**Check compound 3 for convergence**

In 3, the $\text{OH}$ is at C1 and $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is at C3. The ring $\text{C=C}$ can be C1-C2 or C1-C6, but after the second elimination to form the exocyclic $\text{C=CH}_2$ at C3, both routes give the same molecule, 3-methylenecyclohex-1-ene. So only one $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{10}$ product.

**Check compound 2 for divergence**

In 2, the groups are adjacent at C1 and C2. If the ring $\text{C=C}$ forms between C1-C2, the $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ is then attached directly to a $\text{C=C}$ carbon with no H left for exocyclic elimination, leading toward a methylcyclohexadiene type product. If the ring $\text{C=C}$ forms between C1-C6, normal exocyclic elimination is possible, leading to a methylenecyclohexene. Different pathways give different $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{10}$ isomers, so more than one product. Therefore 1 and 3 only qualify.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes compound 2. Compounds 1 and 3 each give a single diene due to symmetry and convergence, but compound 2 can dehydrate in two different directions to give isomeric dienes.
options.B: Correct. Both 1 (1,4-) and 3 (1,3-) give only 4-methylenecyclohex-1-ene and 3-methylenecyclohex-1-ene respectively. In each case alternative positions for the first ring double bond lead to the same final diene, so only one product of formula C7H10 is formed.
options.C: Incorrect. Compound 1 alone is an incomplete answer. Compound 3 also gives only one C7H10 product for the same reason of convergence to a single methylenecyclohexene, so 1 only misses a valid compound.
options.D: Incorrect. Compound 2 is the one that does NOT qualify. Its adjacent OH and CH2OH groups allow the ring double bond to form in two non-equivalent positions, giving more than one C7H10 diene isomer.
